title: Spot a fake job or internship offer
body:
Fake offers target students because students are eager and often new to hiring. These checks catch most of them.

1. Does it ask you to pay? Genuine employers and the AICTE internship portal do not charge students to apply, be selected or be placed. A "registration fee", "security deposit" or "kit fee" is the biggest warning sign.
2. Did you apply? An offer for a job you never applied to, with no interview, is a common way to start a fee request.
3. Where is it happening? Be careful when everything runs through WhatsApp, Telegram, a random form or a shortened link. Look for the employer's own website and email domain. AICTE has warned about fake letters that misuse its name.
4. Is there pressure? "Pay within 2 hours" or "last seat" is meant to stop you from checking.
5. Can you verify it yourself? Search for the company on your own, call its published number, and ask your college placement cell. Do not use the phone number or link in the message to verify the message.

Never share an OTP, card number, PIN or UPI PIN with anyone offering a job. If you have already paid or shared bank details, see the lesson on what to do if you are cheated online.

The Scam checker in the Live area looks for these patterns, but it can never tell you that an offer is genuine.
summary: Five checks that catch most fake offers before you lose money or share private details.
source_title: Alert Regarding Fraudulent Job Appointment Scams Using AICTE and MoE Identities
source_publisher: All India Council for Technical Education

title: What to do if you are cheated online
body:
If money has been taken from you, or you shared bank or UPI details with a stranger, move quickly.

1. Call 1930, the national cyber crime helpline for financial fraud.
2. Tell your bank or wallet provider immediately so they can try to stop further transactions.
3. File a complaint on the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal at cybercrime.gov.in and keep the reference number.
4. Keep evidence: screenshots of chats, the offer letter, the UPI ID or account number you paid, and the receipt. Do not delete the chat.
5. Stop contact with the scammer, and do not pay anything more to "recover" money. Recovery fees are another scam.
6. Tell a trusted adult or your college. Being cheated is not your fault.

If you feel distressed, the Wellbeing page lists free helplines.
summary: The first steps after an online fraud: speed matters.
source_title: National Cyber Crime Reporting Helpline No 1930
